mcqs.q: Class I preparations are for which type of lesion?
mcqs.explain: All pit-and-fissure lesions are Class I.

mcqs.q: Which location is a Class I site?
opts: Occlusal surface of premolars and molars
mcqs.explain: Class I includes occlusal of posteriors, the occlusal two-thirds of facial/lingual surfaces of molars, and the lingual surfaces of maxillary incisors.

mcqs.q: On molars, Class I also includes the:
opts: Occlusal two-thirds of the facial and lingual surfaces (pits/fissures)
mcqs.explain: Class I on molars includes pit/fissure defects in the occlusal two-thirds of the facial and lingual surfaces.

mcqs.q: The objectives of Class I preparation include:
opts: Remove all defects, protect the pulp and withstand masticatory forces
mcqs.explain: As for all preparations: remove defects, protect the pulp and form a preparation that resists fracture under masticatory forces.

mcqs.q: The outline form of a Class I preparation follows:
opts: The pit-and-fissure pattern, including all caries
mcqs.explain: The outline follows the pit-and-fissure pattern, including all caries and weakened enamel, kept as conservative as possible.

mcqs.q: How many walls does a Class I preparation have?
opts: Five (facial, mesial, distal, lingual and pulpal floor)
mcqs.explain: A Class I preparation has five walls: the four surrounding walls (facial, mesial, distal, lingual) and the pulpal floor.

mcqs.q: The floor of a Class I occlusal preparation is the:
mcqs.explain: The pulpal wall/floor is the floor of an occlusal (Class I) preparation, perpendicular to the long axis.

mcqs.q: How many LINE angles does a Class I preparation have?
mcqs.explain: Class I has eight line angles (e.g. mesio-buccal, disto-buccal, bucco-pulpal, etc.).

mcqs.q: How many POINT angles does a Class I preparation have?
mcqs.explain: Class I has four point angles: mesio-/disto-facio-pulpal and mesio-/disto-linguo-pulpal.

mcqs.q: A line angle is formed by the junction of:
mcqs.explain: A line angle is the junction of two walls; a point angle is the junction of three walls.

mcqs.q: The 'bucco-pulpal' line angle is formed by the junction of the:
opts: Buccal (facial) wall and the pulpal floor
mcqs.explain: The bucco-pulpal line angle is the junction of the buccal/facial wall and the pulpal floor.

mcqs.q: For an AMALGAM Class I preparation, the outline:
opts: Includes all the fissures with defined walls
Is limited only to the carious dentin
Is bonded with no defined walls
mcqs.explain: Amalgam (non-bonded) Class I preparations include all fissures with defined walls and a uniform depth.

mcqs.q: An amalgam Class I preparation has a uniform pulpal depth of about:
mcqs.explain: Amalgam Class I preparations are cut to a uniform depth (~1.5–2 mm) to provide bulk/strength for the amalgam.

mcqs.q: Retention in an amalgam Class I preparation is provided by:
mcqs.explain: Amalgam retention comes from occlusal convergence (slight undercut) of the walls; composite relies on bonding.

mcqs.q: The cavosurface margin of an amalgam preparation is typically:
mcqs.explain: Amalgam needs a ~90° cavosurface (butt joint) for bulk/edge strength; composite margins may be bevelled or left.

mcqs.q: A COMPOSITE Class I preparation differs from an amalgam one because it is:
opts: More conservative (caries-only) and retained by bonding
mcqs.explain: Composite preparations are conservative (remove only caries), need no uniform depth or mechanical retention, and rely on bonding.

mcqs.q: Most SMALL Class I lesions today are restored with:
mcqs.explain: Most small Class I restorations are now placed with composite; amalgam is used for larger/high-stress restorations.

mcqs.q: The lingual surfaces of which teeth are Class I sites?
mcqs.explain: The lingual pits of maxillary incisors are Class I (pit-and-fissure) sites.

mcqs.q: The initial entry of a Class I preparation is usually made with a:
mcqs.explain: Initial entry into the tooth is made with a round (or pear-shaped) bur, then the preparation is extended along the fissures.

mcqs.q: A point angle is the junction of:
opts: A wall and the floor only
mcqs.explain: A point angle is the meeting point of three walls (e.g. mesio-facio-pulpal).

mcqs.q: Which is one of the four surrounding (vertical) walls of a Class I preparation?
mcqs.explain: The four surrounding walls are facial, mesial, distal and lingual; the floor is the pulpal wall.

mcqs.q: Compared with amalgam, composite Class I cavosurface margins:
opts: May be bevelled or left without a defined butt joint
mcqs.explain: Composite margins may be bevelled (to increase bonding surface) or left, unlike the strict 90° butt joint needed for amalgam.

saqs.q: List the locations of Class I lesions.
saqs.a: Occlusal of premolars/molars, occlusal two-thirds of facial/lingual of molars, and lingual of maxillary incisors (all pit-and-fissure).

saqs.q: Name the five walls of a Class I preparation.
saqs.a: Facial, mesial, distal, lingual walls and the pulpal floor.

saqs.q: How many line and point angles are there, and what is each?
saqs.a: 8 line angles (junction of two walls) and 4 point angles (junction of three walls).

saqs.q: Differentiate amalgam and composite Class I preparations (outline and retention).
saqs.a: Amalgam: include all fissures, uniform depth, occlusal convergence (retention). Composite: conservative (caries-only), retained by bonding.

saqs.q: What cavosurface margin and depth does an amalgam Class I require?
saqs.a: A ~90° cavosurface (butt joint) and a uniform depth of ~1.5–2 mm for amalgam bulk.

saqs.q: State the objectives of Class I preparation.
saqs.a: Remove all defects, protect the pulp, and withstand masticatory forces without fracture.

saqs.q: What instrument makes the initial entry, and what holds composite in?
saqs.a: Initial entry with a round/pear bur; composite is retained by bonding (no mechanical retention needed).
